brief.notification_title: Black Friday rally caps big week; yields back up
brief.market_summary: US stocks closed Friday's half session higher. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,297, the Nasdaq 2.3% and semis (SMH) 4.2%, finishing a strong week driven by AI stocks. All three indexes are still down for November: the S&P is −5.8% over the month and headed for its worst November since 2008. Treasuries went the other way. The 10Y rose 9bp to 4.94% and the 30Y to 5.33%, ending an eight-day rally. A 25bp hike on 9 Dec is about 96% priced, and the dollar index is above 104. Brent prints range from $90 to $94 depending on source and contract month, so the oil picture is unclear. BTC fell 1.4% to about $59.8k and did not join the equity bounce.
brief.since_last:
- **Session timing:** the US cash market closed Friday's half session at 13:00 ET. The snapshot prices are final for the day, and the next full session is Mon 30 Nov.
- **Stocks:** the AI rebound carried through Black Friday (n14, n9). Breadth widened: over the week, the Russell 2000 rose 3.6% and the Dow 3.4%.
  - Source conflict on the weekly gain: CNBC says the S&P and Dow each rose more than 5% for the week, while the snapshot shows 1W +1.7% and +3.4%. Holiday-week reference points probably explain the gap.
  - The VIX fell to about 24–25, from a 35.89 peak on 20 Nov.
- **Bonds:** yields gave back part of the week's rally. The 10Y went from 4.85% (Treasury par curve, 25 Nov) to 4.94%. The 13-week bill was steady at 4.15%.
- **Policy:**
  - Trump demanded an investigation into the upward Q3 GDP revision (n68, n169).
  - The Fed blackout starts Saturday, so there will be no Fed speakers before the 9 Dec meeting.
- **Oil:** the story shifted to Sunday's OPEC+ meeting. Iraq is pressing for a higher quota (n26, n43), and Reuters reports the US urged Iraq and Venezuela to leave OPEC (n120). Gulf attacks continue (n35).
- **Crypto:** BTC dropped to $58.7k at the US open while stocks rallied (n42). This came after the $7bn options expiry (n5) and alongside record November ETF outflows of about $4.7–5.4bn. JPMorgan says capitulation has been reached (n104).
- **Earnings:** no large-cap US companies reported over the holiday.

sections.summary: An AI-led rebound closed out a strong week in a thin half session. The Nasdaq rose 2.3% and SMH 4.2%. Micron, Broadcom, Amazon and Meta led, along with Anthropic, which rose 11% to $91.88 against its $83 IPO price. The month is still deeply negative: S&P −5.8%, Nasdaq −9.1%, SMH −22.5%. Next week brings ISM, payrolls, MRVL/CRM and Huang's congressional testimony, all with the Fed in blackout.
key_points: Leadership is broadening. One-month returns: XLP +6.8%, XLY +3.9%, XLV +2.4%, versus XLK −16.9%. Defensives and the consumer have been the winners, with tech the laggard.

Nvidia is still down about 28% for November despite the reinstatement rally (n69). Headline risks are piling up: Blackwell racks found in Shanghai, Trump floating a government stake (n32), board lawsuits (n112) and testimony to Congress this week (n109).
Yields rose 9bp on the same day stocks rallied. Equities are rallying against tighter money, which is why I want full-session confirmation.

sections.summary: Treasuries ended an eight-day rally (n135). The 5Y rose 8.6bp to 4.75%, the 10Y 9.0bp to 4.94% and the 30Y 9.3bp to 5.33%, while the 13-week bill held at 4.15%. The hot 3.3% core PCE and a 96%-priced December hike keep the front end pinned. Duration is now trading off growth data and the credibility of US data.
key_points: The 10Y is still 11.4bp lower on the week and 6bp below the 5.00% level where I'd add more IEF. TLT fell 1.2% and IEF 0.4% on the day.
The curve moved roughly in parallel (5Y/10Y/30Y +8.6/+9.0/+9.3bp). 2s10s is about +23–24bp. The 2Y is about 4.70% per CNBC, but its text and table disagree.
Credit is calm: HYG +0.1%, LQD −0.3% (rate-driven). The dollar is above 104, near a 22-month high (n55, n171).
Two cross-currents: Commerzbank sees two hikes (n136), while SEB thinks the 10Y may have peaked (n178). Payrolls on Fri 4 Dec decides which is right.

sections.summary: Brent prints conflict. The snapshot shows $90.34 (−4.5%), AP $90.79, CNBC $93.77 and earlier headlines $94–96. The gap probably reflects contract months around the January expiry. BNO (−0.8% on the day, +0.15% on the week) is the cleaner read: roughly flat on the week, ending three losing weeks, but still −16% to −22% over the month. Sunday's OPEC+ meeting and the Gulf attacks are the drivers.
key_points: Sunday's OPEC+ online meeting is expected to leave Q1 2027 targets unchanged. Iraq wants about 6 mb/d against a 4.431 mb/d ceiling, has raised exports to 3.6 mb/d and is negotiating a higher quota (n26, n43, n154).
Reuters reports the US urged Iraq and Venezuela to leave OPEC (n120). OPEC cohesion risk is bearish for prices over the medium term.

Supply shocks are continuing: Iranian attacks on Hormuz tankers, a Houthi strike on Aramco's Jazan refinery, and fires at Russian, Thai and Venezuelan refineries. ANZ sees a path above $100 (n35). Energy Aspects expects 2027 stockpiling to support prices (n141).
Fuel costs are already doing damage: Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy (n4) and easyJet warns of more airline failures (n40). WTI is $82.96 (−0.9%).

Bottom-calling has started (JPMorgan n104, CZ n16, whale buying n13), but flows haven't turned.

brief.instructor_take: My read is that the market had a very good week, but on thin volume and with weak evidence behind it. Friday's +1.6% S&P and +4.2% SMH happened in a half session, with the Fed going quiet and the macro calendar empty. The full-session tests come next week: ISM Tuesday, MRVL Tuesday night, CRM Wednesday and payrolls Friday. What I'd focus on is that stocks rallied on the same day the 10Y rose 9bp to 4.94%. Core PCE at 3.3% against 3.2% expected, claims at 189K and GDP revised to 4.3% describe an economy that doesn't need help. So the 9 Dec hike is a done deal, and the open question is whether a second hike gets priced. What I think the crowd may be missing is the bond market's credibility problem. When a president calls a GDP revision fake (n68), investors demand more yield to hold long bonds, which is why the 30Y is at 5.33% even after a rally. The other signal I'm watching is bitcoin falling to $58.7k while the Nasdaq rose 2%. That tells me crypto's selling comes from its own flows, so equity strength won't rescue it. My positioning: keep T-bills as the core, hold a measured IEF hedge that I add to only at higher yields, and make semis prove themselves on full-session closes before putting money back in. I'd stay out of crypto until ETF flows turn. I'd change my mind on the defensive tilt if ISM and payrolls come in soft enough to pull the 10Y back below 4.80% while SMH holds above 445.

top_ideas.title: T-bills stay the core into the 9 Dec hike
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills pay 4.15% with a hike 96% priced; keep cash in SGOV
top_ideas.thesis: With the 13-week bill at 4.153% and a 25bp hike about 96% priced for 9 Dec, SGOV earns close to the policy rate with almost no price risk. It also funds the IEF and SMH triggers below. Hot core PCE (3.3%) and 189K claims make a dovish surprise unlikely before the FOMC.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from what the Fed is about to do. The data says the economy is strong and inflation is picking up: core PCE 3.3% vs 3.2% expected, GDP 4.3%, claims 189K. Futures price a hike almost fully. When the policy rate is rising, the front end of the curve resets higher with it, so bills effectively gain from the hike instead of losing value. SGOV beats SHY or longer funds here because its duration is near zero. It earns about 4.15% without the 9bp daily swings we saw in the 5Y on Friday. The concept is carry with no duration: get paid to wait while the uncertainty sits elsewhere. A less experienced investor may see cash as 'missing the rally', but this cash is also the dry powder for the triggers on the other two ideas. I'd turn less enthusiastic if the 13-week fell below 4.0%, or if the FOMC signals this is the last hike, because that would lower the yield I reinvest at.
risks: A pause or final-hike signal at the FOMC lowers reinvestment yields
Opportunity cost if the equity rally broadens and extends
T-bill auction schedule for 30 Nov–4 Dec not confirmed; check TreasuryDirect
top_ideas.entry: Keep the existing position. On Monday, sweep idle cash and any cash set aside for unfilled triggers into SGOV at market. Draw on it only when the IEF or SMH triggers fire.
top_ideas.invalidation: The 13-week yield (now 4.153%) falls below 4.0%, or the 9 Dec FOMC statement or press conference signals a pause or a final hike.
top_ideas.sizing: All idle cash. This is the portfolio's cash sleeve and the funding source for the IEF and SMH tranches.

top_ideas.title: IEF hedge: hold 3%, add only at a 5.00% 10Y
top_ideas.one_liner: 10Y at 4.94%: hold IEF, add 1% only on a 5.00% close
top_ideas.thesis: At about 4.94%, the 10Y offers a real yield cushion and protects the portfolio if next week's data cracks growth or equities sell off after the hike. The case is to buy duration in tranches at higher yields and avoid chasing it on down-yield days, with a hard exit if the 10Y closes above 5.15%.
top_ideas.reasoning: I hold IEF as a hedge, not a bet that yields collapse. If ISM or payrolls disappoint, or the hike hits equities, the 7–10Y part of the curve should rally, and at about 7 years of duration IEF gains roughly 0.7% for every 10bp fall. Friday showed the cost of the trade: hot PCE and a risk-on session pushed the 10Y up 9bp, and tranche 1 near 91.64 is about flat at 91.66. I'm changing one rule. Friday's 10Y finished above my 4.90% ceiling, so tranche 2 didn't trigger. If you don't hold it, buying it at a higher yield is a better entry, not a broken thesis, so I'm widening the band to 4.90–5.05%. I prefer IEF to TLT because the 30Y carries the most term-premium risk from the data-credibility fight (n68), and IEF's smaller drawdowns let the stop do its job. A less experienced investor might keep adding as yields rise. That's why the position is capped at 4% and the 5.15% stop is absolute. A 10Y close above 5.15% would tell me inflation risk is outweighing growth risk, and I would exit the whole position.
catalysts: ISM Manufacturing and JOLTS, Tue 1 Dec
risks: A hot payrolls print with firm wages prices a second hike (n136) and pushes the 10Y through 5.15%
Stocks and bonds fall together if inflation, not growth, is the market's worry
Term-premium pressure from political attacks on official data
top_ideas.entry: Tranche 1 (1.5%, near 91.64): hold. Tranche 2 (1.5%): if you already own it from about 92.06, hold. If you don't, buy on Monday provided the 10Y is between 4.90% and 5.05%. Optional tranche 3 (1%): only on a 10Y close at or above 5.00% before the 9 Dec FOMC. Fund everything from SGOV and cap the position at 4%.
top_ideas.invalidation: A 10Y close above 5.15% exits the whole position. That would put IEF roughly 1.5% below today.
top_ideas.sizing: 3% core, plus an optional 1% at 5.00%. Maximum 4%.

top_ideas.title: Semis: wait for two full-session closes above 445
top_ideas.one_liner: SMH +4% on a half day isn't proof; need 2 full closes >445
top_ideas.thesis: Even after Friday's +4.2% to 440.06, SMH is down 22.5% over the month. The bounce happened in a thin holiday session just before a crowded week of catalysts: MRVL earnings, Huang's testimony to Congress and payrolls. My trigger to start rebuying is unchanged: two consecutive full-session closes above 445.
top_ideas.reasoning: I'll be honest about the cost first. Since the last brief, SMH rose from 422.46 to 440.06, about 4.2%, and this avoid has kept us out of that move. Even so, a 4% gain in a half session that closed at 13:00 ET tells me less than the same gain in a full session would. Holiday liquidity exaggerates moves, and confirmation means price holding through the next full session. The fundamentals behind the bounce are still unsettled. Nvidia is down about 28% for November and faces Blackwell-in-China questions, the possibility of a government stake (n32), board lawsuits (n112) and testimony this week (n109). MRVL reports Tuesday with an implied move of about ±14.8%. On top of that, semis are long-duration growth assets, and the 10Y near 4.94% before a hike weighs on their multiples. If SMH closes above 445 on Monday and Tuesday, I buy half the trimmed amount after MRVL's numbers are out on Wednesday. If it falls back below 400, I stay out through the FOMC.

top_ideas.entry: No semis buying before Monday's full session. The trigger is two consecutive full-session closes above 445; then buy half the previously trimmed amount from SGOV. If MRVL reports between the two closes, buy after its numbers are known. Buy the second half after another week above 445.
top_ideas.invalidation: Two full-session closes above 445 end the avoid. A close below 400 extends it through the 9 Dec FOMC.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new for now. When the trigger fires, half of the previously trimmed semis weight, then the other half a week later.

brief.prior_ideas_review:
1) **SGOV (add): working.** The 13-week yield is 4.153%, versus 4.155% at the last brief, so the carry is intact and no invalidation came close. Keep.

2) **IEF hedge: about flat, with a rule adjustment.**
- Tranche 1 near 91.64 is now 91.66.
- Tranche 2 bought after Wednesday's auction near 92.06 is about 0.4% down.
- Friday's tranche-2 condition (10Y between 4.75% and 4.90%) was not met, because the 10Y finished near 4.94%. If you followed the rule, you correctly didn't buy.
- I'm widening that band to 4.90–5.05% for Monday, because a higher yield is a better entry.
- Tranche 3 at 5.00% is 6bp away. The 5.15% stop is 21bp away.
- Keep.

3) **SMH (avoid): cost us the bounce.** SMH ran from 422.46 to 440.06 (+4.2%), so this avoid has missed upside so far. The trigger hasn't fired, because Friday's half session doesn't count and 445 hasn't been reached. The case for waiting still holds with MRVL and Huang's testimony ahead. Keep the trigger unchanged.

lesson.concept: Thin holiday liquidity and full-session confirmation
lesson.explanation: On holiday-shortened sessions many desks are closed. Volume is light, so a few orders can move prices further than they would on a normal day. Moves still count, but they carry less information about what the broader market believes. That's why I write triggers as 'full-session closes': the price has to hold when the full set of buyers and sellers is present. When a rule says two closes, it filters out noise that would otherwise pull you into a trade too early.
lesson.todays_example: Friday's cash session ended at 13:00 ET. In it, SMH rose 4.2%, the Nasdaq 2.3%, the VIX fell 11% and the 10Y rose 9bp. Brent prints from different sources ranged from about $90 to $96. None of that counts toward the SMH 445 trigger. Monday and Tuesday's full sessions, with ISM and MRVL, are the real test.
